title-group.article-title: Camrelizumab plus apatinib for immune checkpoint inhibitor-naive patients with metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma after first-line tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment failure: a single-arm phase 2 trial

sec.title: Background
sec.p: In the immunotherapy era, tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) monotherapy is still commonly used for patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (RCC) in clinical practice. Prospective evidence on immunotherapy plus tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) after first-line TKI treatment failure is scarce. This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of camrelizumab plus apatinib in this setting.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this single-arm, two-center phase 2 study, patients with metastatic clear cell RCC who had failed first-line TKI treatment were enrolled. Camrelizumab 200 mg once every 2 weeks and apatinib 250 mg once daily were continuously administered until disease progression or intolerable toxicity. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between August 2020 and January 2024, 41 patients were enrolled and treated. Median age was 57.0 years (range, 36–81), and 34 (82.9%) patients were males. By the data cutoff date on December 31, 2024, the median follow-up duration was 19.0 months (range, 3.4–49.4). Median PFS was 11.6 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 6.2–18.5), and the median overall survival was not reached. The objective response rate was 41.5% (95% CI, 26.3%-57.9%). The most common grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were increased alanine aminotransferase (11 [26.8%]), increased aspartate aminotransferase (nine [22.0%]), and proteinuria (nine [22.0%]). No treatment-related deaths occurred.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our findings suggest the potential of camrelizumab plus apatinib in patients with immunotherapy-naïve metastatic RCC after first-line TKI treatment failure, warranting further investigation.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) accounts for about 3% of all adult malignancies, but its global incidence has increased by 2% annually over the past 20 years [1]. Approximately 25%−30% of patients have metastatic RCC at diagnosis. For patients with early-stage RCC, about one-third of them experience relapse with distant metastases after surgery [2]. With the evolution of first-line standard treatment, the value of tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) monotherapy in metastatic RCC has gradually been challenged, especially with the emergence of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapies (programmed cell death-1/ligand 1 [PD-1/PD-L1] inhibitors combined with cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 [CTLA-4] inhibitors or TKIs) [3–7]. However, TKI monotherapy is still a commonly used first-line treatment option in clinical practice [8], primarily due to financial burden and intolerance to combination therapies. After failure of TKI treatment, currently recommended regimens provide unsatisfactory clinical benefits, with a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 4.6–7.4 months [9, 10]. More effective regimens are needed in this setting.

Given that the combination of ICIs and antiangiogenic TKIs has been validated in first-line phase 3 trials [4–7], it may be considered as an ideal option for patients who selected to receive TKI monotherapy without exposure to immunotherapy in the first-line setting. Previous clinical trials have demonstrated the synergistic effect of camrelizumab (anti-PD-1 antibody) combined with apatinib (TKI targeting vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2) in the treatment of several solid tumors [11–14]. Based on the success of the international phase 3 CARES-310 trial [15, 16], camrelizumab plus apatinib has been approved as first-line treatment of unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma in China. This combination also showed promising antitumor activity as second-line treatment in patients with TKI-treated advanced hepatocellular carcinoma [17]. However, its effect in patients with metastatic RCC lacks evidence.
Here we conducted this study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of camrelizumab plus apatinib as second-line treatment in patients with metastatic RCC after first-line TKI treatment failure.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This investigator-initiated phase 2 trial was conducted at two centers in China. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and approved by the ethics committee of Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center and First People's Hospital of Foshan. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study was registered with ChiCTR.org.cn, ChiCTR2000034384.

Patients were eligible if they were aged more than 18 years; had histologically confirmed metastatic clear cell RCC; had progression on or were intolerable to prior first-line TKI therapy; had at least one measurable lesion according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1; had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1; had a life expectancy of more than 12 weeks; and had adequate bone marrow, hepatic, renal, coagulation, and thyroid function. The key exclusion criteria were symptomatic brain metastases requiring steroid therapy or progressive brain metastases; uncontrolled hypertension; prior use of PD-1, PD-L1, or CTLA-4 inhibitors; active autoimmune disease or history of autoimmune disease; history of interstitial lung disease or non-infectious pneumonia; or active pulmonary tuberculosis, hepatitis B, or hepatitis C.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: Patients received camrelizumab 200 mg once every 2 weeks and apatinib 250 mg once a day. Treatment was continued until disease progression, intolerable toxicity, withdrawal of consent, or death. Dose interruptions of both drugs and stepwise dose reductions of apatinib (to 250 mg on days 1–5 of every week and to 250 mg once every other day) were allowed to manage adverse events (AEs). For patients with disease progression, they could restart the study treatment if the investigators judged that these patients could still benefit from camrelizumab plus apatinib.

Imaging examinations (contrast-enhanced computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis) were performed at baseline, every 2 months for the first year, and every 3 months thereafter. Bone scan was performed as needed. Tumor response was evaluated by investigators according to RECIST 1.1. For patients who discontinued the study treatment without progression, tumor assessment was performed every 3 months until disease progression, initiation of new anti-cancer treatment, or death. Survival was followed every 3 months. AEs were monitored throughout the treatment period until 30 days after the last dose of the study treatment, graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.03.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), defined as time from treatment initiation to disease progression or any-cause death. Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR; proportion of patients with the best overall response of complete response [CR] or partial response [PR]), disease control rate (DCR; proportion of patients with the best overall response of CR, PR or stable disease), duration of response (DoR; time from the first CR or PR to disease progression or any-cause death), overall survival (OS; time from treatment initiation to any-cause death), and safety.

sec.title: Statistical analysis of clinical data
sec.p: The historical control of median PFS was 6.7 months [18]. With a two-sided α of 0.05, power of 80%, a hazard ratio of 0.60, an enrollment period of 36 months, and a follow-up period of 12 months, 40 patients were required. Assuming a drop-out rate of 10%, 45 patients should be enrolled.

Efficacy and safety analyses were performed in all patients with at least one dose of the study treatment. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were presented as median (range). PFS, DoR, and OS were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and the 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of their median values were calculated using the Brookmeyer-Crowley method. The 95% CIs of ORR and DCR were calculated using the Clopper-Pearson method. Due to the small sample size, descriptive statistics were used for post-hoc subgroup analyses. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS institute Inc., Cary, NC, United States).

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Between August 2020 and January 2024, 53 patients were screened and 41 were enrolled and received the study treatment (Fig. 1). Given the slow accrual due to the pandemic of coronavirus disease 2019 from 2020 to 2022 and gradually reduced application rate of first-line TKI monotherapy in the two participating centers, the accrual was stopped after enrolling 41 patients (meeting the target sample size without consideration of the drop-out rate). The enrollment duration (41 months) had exceeded expectation (36 months). Baseline characteristics are detailed in Table 1. Of 41 patients, the median age was 57.0 years (range, 36–81), and 34 (82.9%) patients were males. Lung metastases were present in 32 (78.0%) patients, bone metastases in nine (22.0%), and liver metastases in four (9.8%). Thirty-six (87.8%) patients had received prior anti-cancer surgery and three (7.3%) received radiotherapy. Before enrollment, the most commonly used TKI in the first-line setting was sunitinib (24 [58.5%]), followed by pazopanib (13 [31.7%]).

sec.p: By the data cutoff date (December 31, 2024), the median duration of follow-up was 19.0 months (range, 3.4–49.4), and 14 (34.1%) patients were still receiving treatment.

sec.title: Antitumor activity
sec.p: As of the data cutoff date (December 31, 2024), a total of 25 (61.0%) PFS events occurred, and the median PFS was 11.6 months (95% CI, 6.2–18.5; Fig. 2A). Similar PFS benefits were observed in subgroups, except for patients with ECOG performance status of 1 (median, 6.2 months; 95% CI, 1.4-not reached [NR]), bone metastases (median, 6.2 months; 95% CI, 1.4-NR), or lymph node metastases (median, 7.2 months; 95% CI, 6.0–19.1; Fig. 2B). Eleven (26.8%) deaths occurred, and the median OS was NR (95% CI, 23.5-NR).

sec.p: Seventeen of 41 patients achieved PR, with an ORR of 41.5% (95% CI, 26.3%−57.9%), and the DCR was 85.4% (35 of 41; 95% CI, 70.8%−94.4%; Fig. 3A). Median DoR was NR (95% CI, 7.2-NR; Fig. 3B).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Forty (97.6%) of 41 patients experienced at least one treatment-related AE (TRAE), and the incidence of grade ≥ 3 TRAEs was 65.9% (27 of 41; Table 2). The most common TRAEs were proteinuria (34 [82.9%]), increased aspartate aminotransferase (22 [53.7%]), increased alanine aminotransferase (21 [51.2%]), increased blood bilirubin (16 [39.0%]), hyperlipidemia (14 [34.1%]), and hypertension (13 [31.7%]). The most frequent grade ≥ 3 TRAEs were increased alanine aminotransferase (11 [26.8%]), increased aspartate aminotransferase (nine [22.0%]), proteinuria (nine [22.0%]), hypertension (six [14.6%]) and increased blood bilirubin (five [12.2%]). No treatment-related deaths occurred.

fn.p: Data are n (%). Any grade treatment-related adverse events occurred in at least 10% of patients and grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in at least two patients are reported here

sec.p: Owing to TRAEs, 14 (34.1%) patients reduced the dose of apatinib. These TRAEs were transient in three of them. For the other 11 patients, the corresponding TRAEs could be managed by symptomatic treatments and dose reductions. One (2.4%) patient discontinued apatinib alone due to grade 3 drug-induced liver injury, and one (2.4%) discontinued camrelizumab and apatinib due to grade 3 immune-mediated myocarditis.

Regarding hepatotoxicity, all these TRAEs could be reversed by hepatoprotective agents and dose reductions. Hepatotoxicity led to dose reductions of apatinib in two (4.9%) patients, and discontinuation of apatinib treatment in one (2.4%) patient. Liver function returned to normal levels after dose adjustments.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The results of this phase 2 trial provide valuable insights into the efficacy and safety of combining an ICI (camrelizumab) and an antiangiogenic TKI (apatinib) as a second-line treatment option for patients with ICI-naïve metastatic RCC following first-line TKI treatment failure. Median PFS was 11.6 months and the ORR was 41.5%. The toxicity profile was manageable.

In the phase 3 CheckMate 025 and METEOR trials, over 70% of patients with advanced RCC received the study treatment after failure of first-line antiangiogenic TKI treatment, and the median PFS was 4.6 months with nivolumab and 7.4 months with cabozantinib [9, 10]. The subgroup analysis of the METEOR study in patients who previously received only one TKI treatment showed consistent median PFS (7.4 months) [19]. The second-line part of the randomized phase 2 IMmotion150 trial explored the combination of atezolizumab plus bevacizumab in patients with metastatic RCC, with a median PFS of 7.7 months in patients who received first-line sunitinib treatment [20]. In another randomized phase 2 trial, second-line lenvatinib plus everolimus resulted in a median PFS of 14.6 months in patients with metastatic RCC (previous antiangiogenic therapy: 100% TKIs), while second-line lenvatinib monotherapy showed a median PFS of 7.4 months in this population (previous antiangiogenic therapy: 98% TKIs and 2% bevacizumab) [21]. The median PFS in our study (11.6 months) was generally higher than the abovementioned previous reports, and the ORR showed similar trends (41.5% vs. 17%−43%) [9, 10, 19–21]. These results indicate the potential of camrelizumab plus apatinib in this clinical scenario. Given the different clinical settings across studies and the exploratory nature of our study, cautions are needed when interpreting these indirect comparisons. Currently, ICI-based combinations (ICIs plus TKIs or dual ICIs) have become the first-line standard of care for patients with metastatic RCC [3–7]. As access to ICIs continues to expand globally, the population of ICI-naive patients entering the second-line setting is rapidly diminishing. The treatment strategy investigated in our study may be applicable to patients with absolute contraindications to upfront immunotherapy. Previous exploratory clinical trials of camrelizumab plus apatinib for ICI-treated patients showed modest efficacy in advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma but promising antitumor activity in recurrent/metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma [22, 23]. The potential role of this combination as an immunotherapy re-challenge strategy in patients with ICI-treated metastatic RCC requires further investigation.

The toxicity profile of camrelizumab plus apatinib was consistent with previous reports [11–15]. The incidence of grade ≥ 3 AEs with this combination (65.9%) was slightly lower than that with second-line cabozantinib (67%−74%) or lenvatinib plus everolimus (71%) [10, 19, 21]. Despite this, only TRAEs were analyzed in our study while AEs regardless of causality were reported for the other two regimens [10, 19, 21]. The most common grade ≥ 3 AEs were hypertension (15%−16%) and diarrhea (9%−15%) for cabozantinib, and constipation (37%), diarrhea (20%), hypertension (14%), and fatigue or asthenia (14%) for lenvatinib plus everolimus. While diarrhea was not one of the most common grade ≥ 3 AEs for camrelizumab plus apatinib, hypertension (14.6%) was also a major safety concern. In addition, hepatotoxicity (increased alanine aminotransferase: 26.8%; increased aspartate aminotransferase: 22.0%) and proteinuria (22.0%) also required attention. Although these AEs could be well managed by symptomatic treatments and dose adjustments, these results suggest that active monitoring is necessary during treatment with camrelizumab plus apatinib.

Several limitations should be acknowledged in this study. First, this was a single-arm study with a relatively small sample size, which might introduce bias and limit the generalizability of the findings. The subgroup analyses were exploratory and underpowered. Second, the study was designed to enroll 45 patients (accounting for a drop-out rate of 10%) but stopped accrual at 41 patients due to the pandemic of coronavirus disease 2019 and gradually reduced application rate of first-line TKI monotherapy. Despite this, the sample size met the prespecified criteria given that no patients were excluded from the efficacy or safety analysis due to any drop-out events. This reduction in sample size might not affect the statistical power and the precision of the estimated PFS. Finally, follow-up was inadequate to obtain mature OS data. Additional randomized controlled trials with larger cohorts are needed to validate the efficacy and safety of the combination therapy in patients with metastatic RCC.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our findings suggest the potential of camrelizumab plus apatinib as second-line treatment in patients with ICI-naïve metastatic RCC after first-line TKI treatment failure, warranting further validation in randomized controlled trials.
